messages:
lee_patel: Hey team, first day trouble. I started the compose stack but the app fails with `FATAL: password authentication failed for user \"redwood\"`. I didn't touch DB creds, used .env from repo. Any obvious places to look?

anya: Welcome @lee_patel! Two quick checks: 1) Is the DB container actually using the .env values (sometimes compose won't load .env if you run `docker compose` vs `docker-compose` depending on your setup). 2) If the data dir was already initialized, Postgres ignores changes to POSTGRES_PASSWORD in env after first init.

lee_patel: Huh I ran `docker compose up` (Docker Desktop) — does that differ for env loading? I also have a .env.local left over from another project maybe.

michael_s: `docker compose` (new CLI) and `docker-compose` (python one) behave similarly for basics, but env precedence is: shell env -> .env -> env_file entries. If you have .env.local it won't be picked up automatically unless compose references it in env_file. Run `docker compose config` to see resolved envs in the config and `docker compose exec db env | grep POSTGRES` to inspect inside the container.

lee_patel: Ran `docker compose exec db env | grep POSTGRES` and saw POSTGRES_PASSWORD is blank. But my repo .env has POSTGRES_PASSWORD=changeme. Weird.

anya: That usually means either compose didn't load the .env (maybe it's named `.env.example`) or you have an overriding env var locally set to empty. `printenv | grep POSTGRES` on your shell to check. Also check if your shell session exported POSTGRES_PASSWORD as empty.

lee_patel: `printenv` showed nothing. I do have a `.env.local` in my home dir with a different POSTGRES_PASSWORD though. Could that override?

michael_s: Compose doesn't read ~/.env.local by default. But if you launched the process from an IDE that injected envs or if you exported a blank var in your shell rc it could override. Another path: if the container started with an existing data dir, the password won't change even if env has correct value. If the password inside Postgres was set to something else earlier, that'll cause auth failures. Check container logs for `PostgreSQL initdb` messages on first run.

lee_patel: Logs say "database system was shut down; no initdb" which suggests it used an existing PGDATA. I probably ran this stack earlier and then changed .env. How can I fix without losing my local fixtures?

anya: Two routes: 1) If you can afford to reset dev data, move `./pgdata` aside and let the entrypoint init with env creds: `mv ./pgdata ./pgdata.backup && docker compose down && docker compose up -d db`. 2) If you must keep data, connect as superuser inside the container and alter the user's password: `docker compose exec db psql -U postgres -c "ALTER USER redwood WITH PASSWORD 'changeme';"` (replace with the correct password). That requires the container to be running and the postgres superuser password known or that `psql -U postgres` works via peer/local auth inside container.

michael_s: Note: if Postgres was created by a different image version or init scripts changed, manual ALTER may be better. Also, avoid editing `pg_hba.conf` randomly. If you run the ALTER approach, restart the web app after to clear connection pooling.

dev-env-bot: Tip: onboarding guide includes a section on "changing DB creds after init" with recommended reset script that archives data and re-inits. https://redwood.example/docs/onboarding/local-db#change-creds

lee_patel: I tried the ALTER trick: `docker compose exec db psql -U postgres -c "ALTER USER redwood WITH PASSWORD 'changeme';"` and it worked — web app connected after restart. Thanks! I'll back up the pgdata and switch to the reset script approach later.

anya: Nice. If you want, we can pair and add a small check to the README that warns about changing POSTGRES_PASSWORD after initial run. Also welcome aboard! :wave:
